catalog_quote: [V&G 2013:101-102] Stress occurs once per word. Regular stress occurs on the second syllable of the word, as in /mi.ˈka.ra.waɁ/ ‘turkey’. However, word-final stress is avoided, causing disyllabic words to have initial stress, as in /ˈsi.sɘk/ ‘porcupine’, except when there is no other syllable available, as in /ˈɲɘk/ ‘the place I used to live’. A marginal pattern is final syllable stress in polysyllables, occurring in /wi.ˈa/ (approximately [wˈja]) ‘squirrel’ and /si.ˈmir/ ‘Varadero (place name)’, while /ˈin.ka.tuʔ/ ‘four’ has exceptional stress on the first syllable. Incorporated verbs, nominal compounds and many suffixed forms are treated as single words, as in /ˈi.kɘr/ ‘hurt’ + /ˈmutuɁ/ ‘head’ + /ˈlɘk/ ‘1SG’ giving /i.ˈkɘr.mu.tuɁ.lɘk/ ‘I have a headache’ ... Again, suffixing /ˈu.ru/ ‘deer’ with the diminutive /ʃa/ gives regular /u.ˈru.ʃa/ ‘small deer’; adding delimitative /-saɁ/ retains the accent on the second syllable, /u.ˈru.ʃa.saɁ/ ‘only a small deer’. However, some suffixes impose other stress patterns, outlined in the remainder of this section. [Madalengoitia 2013:61-62] El jebero es una lengua con acento fijo, es decir, una lengua en la que la posición del acento es predecible, pues responde a la aplicación de una regla. ... El acento en jebero siempre se posiciona en la primera sílaba si la palabra es bisilábica, y en la segunda contando de izquierda a derecha si la palabra posee más de dos sílabas
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Stress occurs once per word. Regular stress occurs on the second syllable of the word, as in /mi.ˈka.ra.waɁ/ ‘turkey’. However, word-final stress is avoided, causing disyllabic words to have initial stress, as in /ˈsi.sɘk/ ‘porcupine’, except when there is no other syllable available, as in /ˈɲɘk/ ‘the place I used to live’. A marginal pattern is final syllable stress in polysyllables, occurring in /wi.ˈa/ (approximately [wˈja]) ‘squirrel’ and /si.ˈmir/ ‘Varadero (place name)’, while /ˈin.ka.tuʔ/ ‘four’ has exceptional stress on the first syllable.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (10 pp., native text, Cambridge Core copy with doi:10.1017/S0025100312000370 on p. 1). The section headed "Stress" begins at the foot of journal p. 101 (p. 5) and continues on p. 102 (p. 6); the quoted passage from "Stress occurs once per word" through "has exceptional stress on the first syllable" is there word for word, including the transcriptions /mi.ˈka.ra.waɁ/, /ˈsi.sɘk/, /ˈɲɘk/, /wi.ˈa/, /si.ˈmir/, /ˈin.ka.tuʔ/. The remainder of the section (compounds/incorporation as single words; desiderative /ja/, locative /k~kɘk/, participial /an/, emphatic /un.ˈta.na/, regret particle /tʃi/) and the Intonation section on p. 103 (falling pitch accent on every stressed syllable, question pa…
new_statements.rule_in_words: One stress per word, on the second syllable from the left; because final stress is avoided, disyllables are stressed on the first syllable and monosyllables on their only syllable. Madalengoitia 2013 (pp. 61-64) states the same rule in Spanish ('El acento en jebero siempre se posiciona en la primera sílaba si la palabra es bisilábica, y en la segunda contando de izquierda a derecha si la palabra posee más de dos sílabas') and analyses it as left-to-right trochees with an initial extrametrical syllable in 3+-syllable words and a ban on degenerate feet.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in either source; V&G say stress occurs once per word and that longer words with regret particles may keep the original stress plus the imposed one (/ka.ˈlu.wiɁ.pa.ˈʎi tʃi/, p. 105).
new_statements.exceptions: Marginal final stress in a few polysyllables (/wi.ˈa/ 'squirrel', /si.ˈmir/ 'Varadero'); /ˈin.ka.tuʔ/ 'four' initial; desiderative prefix /ja-/ attracts stress; locative /-k/ ~ /-kɘk/ attracts stress on mono/disyllabic bases; 3SG participial /-an/ attracts stress on monosyllabic verbs; emphatic /un.ˈta.na/ inherently stressed; regret particles /tʃi/ (male), /tɘn/ (female) and question particles /aɁ.tʃa/, /aɁ.taɁ/ shift stress in the preceding word. Bendor-Samuel (1981:36, via Madalengoitia 2013 p. 62) reports penultimate stress with suffixes -a'cha, -a'ta', -chi, -ten, -untana.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word; compounds, incorporated verbs and most suffixed forms count as single words (/i.ˈkɘr.mu.tuɁ.lɘk/ 'I have a headache'). Stressed syllables carry falling pitch accents, one per word, not reduced by information structure (Intonation section, pp. 104-105). Madalengoitia's domain is the root/word in citation forms, with F0 rise on the stressed vowel.
new_statements.identity_note: All three opened sources describe the Shiwilu of Jeberos village (District of Jeberos, Alto Amazonas, Loreto), the only surviving variety of jebe1250; V&G 2013 speakers born 1935/1940 in Jeberos; Madalengoitia's data from Proyecto Cahuapana speakers in Jeberos. 'Jebero' and 'Shiwilu' are the same language (ISO jeb).

new_statements.quote: All words except compound words contain one stressed syllable. [...] Except for instances described later in this section and in sections 3444 and 3445, the stressed syllable of any simple word is always as follows: a) for monosyllabic words the stressed syllable is always the one and only syllable, b) for bi-syllabic words the stressed syllable is always the first syllable, c) for words of three or more syllables the stressed syllable is always the second syllable.

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the catalog stress on syllable 1 of 2, 2 of 3, 2 of 4 and as Valenzuela & Gussenhoven 2013 (second syllable, disyllables initial); adds the 1958 field description of the exceptional classes (verbs in -aŋ, nominals in -k, penultimate stress with word suffixes -aʔca/-aʔtɘʔ/-ci/-tɘŋ/-untana, emphatic stress), which correspond to V&G 2013's /an/, /k/, /untana/ and /tʃi/ cases. The '1979' date in the Glottolog citation is not on the document: the ILV print is dated 1981 (title page), the thesis May 1958; works 0, 1 and 2 are one and the same document.
new_statements.rule_in_words: One stressed syllable per simple word: monosyllables are stressed, disyllables on the first syllable, words of three or more syllables on the second syllable (i.e. second-syllable stress with final stress avoided in disyllables). Stress is realized by prominence (loudness/force), length and higher pitch on the stressed syllable (§3.4.4.2, p. 35).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described; the author states each simple word contains exactly one stressed syllable. Compound words carry a stressed syllable on the initial syllable of each reduplicated root plus one on the second syllable of the post-root elements (first if those elements have fewer than three syllables) (p. 35). 'Emphatic stress' (§3.4.4.5, p. 36) may fall on any syllable and then replaces word stress.
new_statements.exceptions: p. 36: (a) any bisyllabic verb of a monosyllabic stem + inflectional suffix -aŋ is stressed on the second (final) syllable (ɬi'aŋ 'seeing', wer'aŋ 'stinging'); (b) any nominal of a bisyllabic stem + non-verbal suffix -k (form of -kek) is stressed on the second syllable (ta'nak 'in the jungle', pi'dɘk 'in the house'); (c) 'word suffix stress' §3.4.4.4: words carrying the word suffixes -aʔca, -aʔtɘʔ, -ci, -tɘŋ, -untana are stressed on the penultimate syllable of the resulting word (asumpa'laʔnca 'have you tied up', ipiʔ'maci 'now indeed'); (d) emphatic stress on any syllable, preferentially on the first vowel of the extensor -apa-.
new_statements.identity_note: Bendor-Samuel describes the Jebero language of the village of Jeberos between the Marañón and Huallaga rivers, NE Peru (about 1,500 speakers in 1958; Chapter 1, thesis p. 1 = p. 11), i.e. the same language as the catalog's Shiwilu (jebe1250, ISO jeb); he warns not to confuse it with Jivaro. No dialect distinction is made.

new_statements.quote: Two types of word stress which fall outside the patterns described so far in this section are as follows: a) any bi-syllabic verb form comprising a monosyllabic stem and the inflectional suffix -aŋ, § 7432, is stressed on the second syllable. [...] b) Any nominal comprising a bi-syllabic stem and the non-verbal suffix -k, which is one form of the suffix -kek, § 833, is stressed on the second syllable. [...] 3444 Word suffix stress. In all words which are suffixed by the word suffixes listed below, the stressed syllable is the penultimate syllable of the resultant word. The word suffixes involved in this type of stress pattern are: -aʔca, -aʔtɘʔ, -ci, -tɘŋ, -untana

sources.note: §3.2 Patrón acentual pp. 61-64: 'El jebero es una lengua con acento fijo'; stress on the first syllable of disyllables and on the second syllable of words of three or more syllables (Tabla 30); metrical analysis with left-to-right trochees, initial extrametrical syllable in 3+-syllable words, no degenerate feet; acknowledges Bendor-Samuel's suffix-triggered penultimate stress (-a'cha, -a'ta', -chi, -ten, -untana) but could not corroborate; F0 rise on the stressed syllable (Figs. 6-7). Conclusion 2.2 p. 76 restates.
